analysis.one_liner: Requires electronics makers to share repair manuals, parts, and tools with independent repair shops.
analysis.headline: The Fair Repair Act was introduced in the Senate in May 2024 with two sponsors, sent to the Commerce Committee, and never received a vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require makers of digital electronic equipment—phones, laptops, appliances, and similar products—to sell repair documentation, parts, and diagnostic tools to independent repair shops and device owners on the same terms they offer their own authorized repair services. It would also ban the common practice of "parts pairing," where software disables a device or cuts its performance when a non-manufacturer part is installed. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the rules. Car manufacturers and medical device makers are carved out.
analysis.who_benefits: Device owners, who could get their phones, laptops, and appliances fixed at independent shops instead of paying manufacturer prices or replacing broken devices; and independent repair businesses, which gain access to the manuals, parts, tools, and security codes they currently cannot get.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Device owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers must make documentation, parts, and tools—including software needed to reset security locks—available to owners and independent repair providers on fair and reasonable terms, defined as no worse than the best terms offered to the manufacturer's own authorized repair providers.

The bill bans parts pairing and similar mechanisms that disable otherwise-functional replacement parts, reduce a device's performance after an independent repair, display false or non-dismissible warnings, or raise the price of future repairs.
The FTC can enforce the bill as an unfair or deceptive practice, and state attorneys general can sue in court to stop violations, collect civil penalties, and win restitution for state residents.

analysis.who_pays: Consumer electronics and appliance manufacturers, which would have to sell repair information and parts at non-preferential terms and lose a lever that steers customers back to their own repair services and pushes owners toward buying new devices.

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts motor vehicles and medical devices entirely, so two of the areas where repair restrictions are most contested—farm equipment and hospital machinery, in the case of medical devices—are left out of this version.

A trade-secret provision lets manufacturers withhold information they classify as a trade secret except when needed to supply documentation, parts, or tools on fair terms, which could invite disputes over what must be shared.

Manufacturers argue that forced sharing of diagnostic software and security-reset tools could weaken device security, an objection raised against right-to-repair laws generally; the bill responds by requiring makers to provide security-lock reset tools but does not eliminate the debate.
Non-manufacturer parts and repairs could raise genuine safety and quality questions for some equipment, which is why the exclusions and trade-secret carve-outs exist.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most owners, the benefits are concrete: cheaper repairs, longer device life, and an end to software that punishes independent fixes. The main costs fall on manufacturers, whose repair and replacement business is the point of the bill. The design has real gaps—cars and medical devices are excluded—so consumers in those categories get nothing here, but for the devices it covers the terms are clearly defined and enforcement is straightforward.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2024, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no action until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Ben Ray Luján introduced the bill in the Senate on May 23, 2024, joined by Sen. Ron Wyden.
The same day it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, where it remained for the rest of the Congress.
The bill never advanced past committee, never received a hearing or a floor vote, and expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Electronics and appliance manufacturers are better off: the restrictions on parts pairing, on steering repairs through authorized channels, and on repair-part pricing never took effect, so device owners keep paying manufacturer repair and replacement prices.

for.name: Sen. Ben Ray Luján
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Mexico; introduced the Fair Repair Act
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on May 23, 2024, and referred it to the Commerce Committee.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor; the bill was introduced on his behalf with Luján.

sides.party_line_note: Both Senate supporters were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill died in committee without attracting broader support or organized opposition in the record.

industries.note: The bill would force them to sell repair documentation, parts, tools, and security-reset software to anyone on terms equal to their authorized repair shops, and would ban parts pairing that degrades independently repaired devices. Their gain from the status quo—steering repairs through their own channels and pushing owners toward new purchases—is what the bill takes away.

Repair shops would get the manuals, diagnostic tools, parts, and security codes they are currently denied, letting them compete directly with manufacturer repair services. Their growth in business comes from lower repair prices for device owners.

industries.industry: Authorized repair networks and device resellers
industries.note: Authorized repair providers keep their existing warranty and recall arrangements with manufacturers, which the bill explicitly protects, but they would face competition from independents now operating on equal terms. Device resellers of used equipment benefit from the bill's protection of repairs on products already in use.

industries.industry: Motor vehicle and medical device manufacturers
industries.note: The bill explicitly exempts motor vehicle manufacturers, motor vehicle equipment makers, and medical device makers, so repair restrictions in those sectors would be untouched. This carve-out was a key concession in right-to-repair fights over cars and hospital equipment.
